stem: What does this excerpt mainly show about Teodor?
stimulus:
The following text is from Hanne Ostrova's 1911 novel The Winter Conservatory. Teodor, a young cellist, is listening to his teacher, Mr. Lind, play.

Mr. Lind drew the bow slowly, and the low note filled every corner of the cold room. The other students nodded politely, as they always did. Teodor, however, sat forward with his hands clenched in his lap. He was not listening to a lesson. He was listening to the sound he had wanted to make for as long as he could remember, and he could not yet make it.
choices: Teodor longs to make the sound his teacher can make.
Mr. Lind is proud of how closely his students listen.
Teodor is bored by a lesson he has heard before.
Teodor first heard a cello at a concert as a child.
explanation: The setup line tells you Teodor is the focus. Everything after 'however' is about him: he leans forward, clenches his hands, and wants a sound he 'could not yet make.' Put simply, he longs to play the way his teacher plays. Naming the right person and the right feeling in plain words is the step you need before you can answer a real 'main purpose of a literary excerpt' question, where the right choice will say something like 'To portray a student's longing...'

B.why: You moved the focus from Teodor to Mr. Lind. The teacher is in the scene, but the excerpt never shows what he feels. It shows what Teodor feels while he listens.

C.why: You may have mixed Teodor up with the other students, who nod politely. The word 'however' sets Teodor apart from them. He is leaning forward and gripping his hands, which is the opposite of bored.

D.why: The text says he has wanted the sound 'for as long as he could remember,' but it never says where or when he first heard a cello. You added a detail the excerpt does not give.

stem: What does this excerpt mainly show about the narrator?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ilse Marrow's 2004 novel The Field Recordings. The narrator, a linguistics student, is recording her grandmother's speech.

I had come with a microphone and a list of words to check: the old local names for a wheelbarrow, a puddle, the first frost. Gran answered each one patiently. But somewhere around the word for "puddle," I stopped writing. She was telling me about the lane where she had splashed as a girl, and I realized I wanted the story far more than the word.
choices: Gran grows tired of answering her granddaughter's long list of questions.
The narrator learns the old local word that Gran used for a puddle.
The narrator comes to value Gran's memories more than her word list.
The narrator's professor had asked her to record twenty local words.
explanation: The setup line makes the narrator the focus. The excerpt starts with her research plan, then turns at 'But': she stops writing and wants 'the story far more than the word.' So the excerpt shows her caring more about her grandmother's memories than about her list. Saying what the whole excerpt shows about the focus person is the first step in any 'main purpose of a literary excerpt' question.

A.why: You moved the focus to Gran and got her reaction wrong. The text says she answered 'patiently.' Nothing suggests she is tired.

B.why: You picked a single detail and missed what the excerpt as a whole shows. The puddle word only marks the moment she stops writing. What matters is that the story comes to matter more to her than the word.

D.why: The excerpt never mentions a professor or a number of words. You added a background detail that the text does not give.

stem: What is this poem mainly trying to do for the person it speaks to?
stimulus:
The following text is from Rowan Ashby's 1923 poem "To a Young Birder."

Do not be troubled that the marsh is still,
That every reed looks empty to your eye.
Sit longer. Let the cold come through your coat.
The heron you were promised is nearby,
And patience is the only kind of call
A wary bird will ever answer to.
choices: To warn a young birder that the cold marsh is a dangerous place
To urge a young birder to keep waiting quietly for a shy bird
To describe the first heron the speaker ever saw as a child
To describe the reeds and plants that grow in a quiet marsh
explanation: The title names the person the poem speaks to: a young birder. The speaker says 'Do not be troubled,' 'Sit longer,' and promises the heron is 'nearby.' That is encouragement to be patient. Working out who is being spoken to and what tone the speaker uses is the step you need for a real 'main purpose of a poem' question, where the right choice usually starts 'To encourage...' or 'To convey...'

A.why: You flipped the tone. The cold is mentioned only as something to put up with while waiting ('Let the cold come through your coat'). The poem is reassuring the birder, not warning them away.

C.why: The poem never tells a story about the speaker's own past. The heron it mentions is one the birder is about to see. You added a memory that is not in the text.

D.why: The reeds are background. The poem is speaking to a person and telling them what to do. A choice that only describes the setting misses the poem's purpose.

stem: What does this excerpt mainly show about the narrator as a child?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Corin Hale's 1998 memoir Station Weather. The narrator's father worked as a weather observer on a small island.

Every three hours, my father climbed the hill to read the instruments, and every three hours I begged to go with him. He said the wind up there could knock a child flat. I believed him, and I went on begging anyway. To me, the white box of thermometers on the hilltop was the most important place in the world, and I wanted to stand beside it.
choices: The father was proud of keeping careful records of the island's weather.
The narrator was too frightened of the wind to climb the hill.
The narrator grew up to become a weather scientist like the father.
The narrator badly wanted to join the father in his weather work.
explanation: The setup and the stem make the young narrator the focus. The narrator 'begged' every three hours, kept begging even after the warning, and calls the instrument box 'the most important place in the world.' So the excerpt shows a child who badly wants to be part of the father's work. Naming the right person and the right wish is what you will do first on a real 'main purpose of a literary excerpt' question.

A.why: You moved the focus from the child to the father. The father's routine is the backdrop, but the excerpt is about what the child wants, not about how the father feels about his records.

B.why: The narrator believed the warning but 'went on begging anyway.' That shows wanting to go, not being too afraid to go. You reversed the narrator's reaction.

C.why: The excerpt stays in the narrator's childhood and never says what career came later. You assumed an outcome the text does not give.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Clara Wendt's 1931 memoir about growing up on a wheat farm. Here, Wendt describes her father after a county agricultural agent tested the soil in one of his fields.

For thirty years my father had believed that the low field was simply tired ground. He planted it last and expected little from it. But the agent's test showed that the soil lacked only lime. That evening my father walked the field twice, kneeling every few rows to crumble the earth in his hands. At supper he spoke of nothing but spring, and he laughed more than I had heard him laugh in years.
choices: To convey the narrator's admiration for the county agent's skill at testing soil
To describe the method the agent used to measure the minerals in the soil
To portray the father's renewed hope after learning the low field could be improved
To convey the father's doubt that the low field could ever produce good crops
explanation: The setup line says the focus is your father, so ask what the whole excerpt shows about him. He had written the field off. Then he learns it only needs lime, walks it twice, talks about spring, and laughs. Put plainly, he feels hopeful again, and that matches C. This is the core move for every main-purpose question about a literary excerpt: find who the setup puts in focus, say in plain words what the excerpt shows about that person, then pick the choice with the right person and the right feeling.

A.why: You moved the focus to the wrong person. The agent is mentioned only once, and the narrator never praises the agent. The setup and every sentence after it are about the father's reaction. Picking a minor character's role over the main person's feeling is this subtype's main trap.

B.why: You picked a detail the text never gives. The excerpt says only that the test found the soil lacked lime. It doesn't say how the test was done or which minerals were measured. A choice naming a concrete detail the passage leaves out can't be its purpose.

D.why: You turned the tone around. The father doubted the field only before the test. The excerpt is built around how that doubt goes away: he walks the field, talks of spring, and laughs. 'Doubt' describes the old belief the passage overturns, not what the passage conveys.
